summary: Specifies the syntax and processing of an Evidence Record, a structure for supporting long-term proof that data existed and was unchanged, including signed data, over a long and uncertain period. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4998 defines the Evidence Record Syntax, a structure for proving that some data existed at a particular time, and for keeping that proof usable for decades. It holds a set of timestamps over a tree of hashes of the archived files, so one file can be proved without the others. When the hashing or signing algorithms start to weaken, the timestamps are renewed by timestamping the old ones, or by timestamping the data and the old timestamps together.

questions: how to prove data existed long term
subtitle: A structure for proving that a document existed years ago, and for keeping that proof usable as the cryptography ages.

tldr.problem: A digital signature proves that data was signed and has not changed, but that proof weakens over time: the hash algorithm or the public key algorithm can become weak, or the certificate can expire. A document that must be provable in thirty years needs something that is renewed before the cryptography underneath it fails.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an Evidence Record, an ASN.1 structure holding archive timestamps. Each archive timestamp is a timestamp over the root of a Merkle hash tree whose leaves are the hashes of the archived objects, plus the reduced tree needed to prove one object. When the cryptography weakens, the timestamps are renewed in one of two ways: timestamp renewal, which timestamps the old timestamp, or hash-tree renewal, which timestamps the data and the old timestamps again.
tldr.outcome: The result is a standardised way to keep a non-repudiable proof of existence alive over a long archival period, usable with a single file or carried inside a signed message. The RFC says nothing about how to talk to an archive service, and warns that the record should be duplicated with different algorithms and different authorities.

today: RFC 4998 is a Proposed Standard from August 2007 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It defines the ASN.1 module for evidence records, and its syntax rests on the timestamp protocol of RFC 3161 and the message syntax of RFC 3852. The document says it does not specify a protocol for interacting with a long-term archive system, which was left to the IETF Long-Term Archive Network Services working group, and it is designed to meet the requirements of RFC 4810.

sections.title: Motivation: Proving That Data Existed
sections.content:
In many application areas of electronic data exchange, a non-repudiable proof of the existence of digital data has to be possible, and in some cases that proof must survive the passage of long periods of time. An important example is digitally signed data. Digital signatures demonstrate data integrity and authenticate the source, and in some cases signed data must be archived for 30 years or more.

The reliability of digital signatures over long periods is not absolute. During the archival period, hash algorithms and public key algorithms can become weak, or certificates can become invalid, and these events complicate the reliance on digitally signed data after many years by increasing the likelihood that forgeries can be created. To avoid losing the security properties that come from digital signatures, it is necessary to prove that the signed data already existed before such a critical event. A timestamp can do that, but some timestamps rely on mechanisms that will be subject to the same problems. To counter this, timestamps are renewed by obtaining a new timestamp that covers the original data and its earlier timestamps, before the mechanisms used to generate them are compromised.

The document therefore standardises the data formats and processing procedures for such timestamps, so that preservation evidence can be verified and communicated. A first approach was made in the IETF by RFC 3126, which specified an optional Archive Timestamp Attribute for integration into signatures according to the Cryptographic Message Syntax. Evidence Record Syntax broadens and generalises that approach to data of any format and takes the requirements of long-term archive services into account, in particular the handling of large sets of data objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature shows that a document was signed and has not been altered. Over decades that proof can weaken, because the algorithms it rests on get weaker or the certificate expires. This RFC defines a way of proving the document existed, and of re-proving it before the cryptography underneath it fails.

sections.title: Overview and the Two Kinds of Renewal
sections.content:
ERS is designed to meet the data structure requirements set out in RFC 4810. Its basis is the Archive Timestamp, which can cover a single data object, as an RFC 3161 compliant timestamp does, or a group of data objects. Groups of data objects are addressed using hash trees, first described by Merkle, combined with a timestamp. The leaves of the hash tree are hash values of the data objects in the group, and a timestamp is requested only for the root hash of that tree. The deletion of a data object in the tree does not influence the provability of others, and for any particular data object the hash tree can be reduced to a few sets of hash values that are sufficient to prove its existence. The tree can also be reduced to prove the existence of a data group, provided all members of the group have the same parent node in the tree.

An Evidence Record may contain many Archive Timestamps. Before the cryptographic algorithms used within an Archive Timestamp become weak, or timestamp certificates become invalid, Archive Timestamps have to be renewed by generating a new one. ERS distinguishes two ways of doing that.

Timestamp renewal is necessary if the private key of a Timestamping Unit has been compromised, or if an asymmetric algorithm or a hash algorithm used for the generation of the timestamps is no longer secure for the given key size. The timestamp of an Archive Timestamp is hashed and timestamped by a new Archive Timestamp. This mode can be used when it is not necessary to access the archived data objects covered by the timestamp, which makes it very efficient, in particular when archiving is done by a service that manages Archive Timestamps centrally.

Timestamp renewal is not sufficient if the hash algorithm used to build the hash tree of an Archive Timestamp becomes insecure. Then hash-tree renewal is required, and all the evidence data must be accessed and timestamped again. This includes not only the timestamps but also the complete Archive Timestamps and the archived data objects covered by them, which must be hashed and timestamped again by a new Archive Timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to refresh the proof, and the choice depends on what has gone stale. If the signing key or the signing algorithm is the problem, a new timestamp can simply cover the old timestamp. If the hashing algorithm is the problem, the data itself has to be hashed and timestamped again.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document defines the terms the rest of it uses. An archived data object is a data unit that is archived and has to be preserved for a long time by the Long-term Archive Service. An archived data object group is a set of two or more data objects that for some reason belong together, for example a document file and a signature file, which together represent signed data.

An Archive Timestamp is a timestamp and typically lists of hash values, which allow the verification of the existence of several data objects at a certain time. In its most simple variant, when it covers only one object, it may consist of the timestamp alone.

An Archive Timestamp Chain is a time-ordered sequence of Archive Timestamps in which each Archive Timestamp preserves the non-repudiation of the previous one, even after that previous Archive Timestamp becomes invalid. Overall non-repudiation is maintained until the new Archive Timestamp itself becomes invalid, and the process of generating such a chain is called Timestamp Renewal. An Archive Timestamp Sequence is a sequence of Archive Timestamp Chains in which each chain preserves the non-repudiation of the previous chains, even after the hash algorithm used within the previous Archive Timestamp's hash tree became weak. Non-repudiation is preserved until the last Archive Timestamp of the last chain becomes invalid, and the process of generating such a sequence is called Hash-Tree Renewal.

A reduced hash tree is the process of reducing a Merkle hash tree to a list of lists of hash values, and it is the basis of storing the evidence for a single data object. A timestamp is a cryptographically secure confirmation generated by a Time Stamping Authority; RFC 3161 specifies a structure for timestamps and a protocol for communicating with such an authority, and other data structures and protocols may also be appropriate.

An Evidence record is the collection of evidence compiled for one or more given archived data objects over time. It includes all the Archive Timestamps, within the structures of chains and sequences, and additional verification data such as certificates, revocation information, trust anchors, policy details and role information. A Long-term Archive Service is a service responsible for preserving data for long periods of time, including generation and collection of evidence, and storage of archived data objects and evidence.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names the pieces: the archived files, the timestamps over them, the chain of timestamps that renews each other, and the sequence of chains that survives the failure of the hashing algorithm.

sections.title: The Evidence Record Syntax
sections.content:
An Evidence Record is a unit of data that can be used to prove the existence of an archived data object, or of an archived data object group, at a certain time. It contains the Archive Timestamps generated during a long archival period, and possibly further data useful for validation. It can be stored separately from the archived data objects or integrated into the data itself, and the appendix of the RFC gives the rules for signed and enveloped data in the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

The ASN.1 syntax is:

EvidenceRecord ::= SEQUENCE {
   version                   INTEGER { v1(1) } ,
   digestAlgorithms          SEQUENCE OF AlgorithmIdentifier,
   cryptoInfos               [0] CryptoInfos OPTIONAL,
   encryptionInfo            [1] EncryptionInfo OPTIONAL,
   archiveTimeStampSequence  ArchiveTimeStampSequence
   }

The version field indicates the syntax version, for compatibility with future revisions and to distinguish the record from earlier, non-conformant or proprietary versions. The value 1 indicates this specification, lower values indicate an earlier version, and an implementation conforming to this specification should reject a version below 1.

digestAlgorithms is the union of all the hash algorithms used to hash the data objects over the archival period, taken from the Archive Timestamps in the record; the order of the values is not relevant. cryptoInfos allows data useful in the validation of the archive timestamp sequence to be stored, such as trust anchors, certificates, revocation information, or the current definition of the suitability of cryptographic algorithms, past and present, for example RSA 768-bit valid until 1998, RSA 1024-bit valid until 2008, or SHA1 valid until 2010. These items may be added according to the policy used, and because this data is not protected within any timestamp, it should be verifiable through other mechanisms, which is outside the scope of the document. encryptionInfo holds the information needed to support encrypted content, and archiveTimeStampSequence is the sequence of Archive Timestamp Chains.
sections.plainLanguage: The record has four parts: a version number, the list of hash algorithms used over the years, optional extra material for checking the record, optional information for encrypted data, and the sequence of timestamp chains that carries the proof itself.

sections.title: The Archive Timestamp and Its Hash Tree
sections.content:
An Archive Timestamp is a timestamp and a set of lists of hash values. The lists are generated by reducing an ordered Merkle hash tree whose leaves are the hash values of the data objects to be timestamped. Every inner node of the tree contains one hash value, generated by hashing the concatenation of its children, and the root hash value, which represents unambiguously all the data objects, is the one that is timestamped.

The tree is built in five steps. Collect the data objects to be timestamped. Choose a secure hash algorithm H and generate hash values for the data objects, which become the leaves. For each data group containing more than one document, sort the document hashes in ascending binary order, concatenate them and hash them, keeping the complete output of the hash algorithm, so leading zeros are not removed, with the most significant bit first. If there is more than one hash value, place them in groups and sort each group in ascending binary order, concatenate and hash them to get the inner nodes, and repeat until only one hash value is left, the root node. Then obtain a timestamp for that root hash value, using the same hash algorithm as the hash tree, unless the digestAlgorithm field of the Archive Timestamp is present and names it.

The tree is then reduced to the lists needed to prove one data object. Hash the data object with H to get a value h. Select all the hash values that have the same father node as h, arrange them in ascending binary order, and store them as one partial hash tree. Repeat that step for the father node of all those hashes until the root hash is reached. The father nodes themselves are not saved, because they can be computed. The list of all the partial hash trees is the reduced hash tree. The RFC notes that there are no restrictions on the quantity or length of the hash value lists, and that building and reducing hash trees is profitable but not required, since an Archive Timestamp may consist of only one list of hash values and a timestamp, or of only a timestamp with no hash value lists at all.

Verification runs the other way. Calculate the hash value h of the data object with the algorithm given in the digestAlgorithm field, or the digest algorithm of the timestamp if that field is not present. Search for h in the first list of the reduced hash tree; if it is not there, verification ends with a negative result. Concatenate the hash values of that list in ascending binary order and calculate the hash value h', which must be a member of the next higher list, and continue until the root hash value is calculated. Finally check the timestamp: for an RFC 3161 timestamp the root hash value must correspond to the hashedMessage field, and the digest algorithm to the hashAlgorithm field, both in the messageImprint field of the timeStampToken.
sections.plainLanguage: Each archived file is hashed, and the hashes are combined two at a time into a tree, with one hash at the top. Only that top hash is timestamped. To prove one file later, the verifier needs the hashes of its siblings on the way up, and recomputes the same chain of hashes until it reaches the timestamped value.

sections.title: Chains, Sequences and Their Verification
sections.content:
An Archive Timestamp proves the existence of data at a certain time, but the first one in the first chain can become invalid when the hash or public key algorithms used in its hash tree or timestamp become weak, or when the validity period of the timestamp authority certificate expires or is revoked. Before such an event, the existence of the Archive Timestamp or of the archive-timestamped data has to be reassured by creating a new Archive Timestamp, and the kind of renewal depends on whether the timestamp or the hash algorithm became weak.

In a timestamp renewal, the content of the timeStamp field of the old Archive Timestamp is hashed and timestamped by a new Archive Timestamp. The new Archive Timestamp may omit the reduced hash tree if the timestamp only simply covers the previous timestamp, but generally a number of old Archive Timestamps can be collected and a new hash tree built with the hash values of the content of their timeStamp fields. The new Archive Timestamp is added to the chain, and its hash tree must use the same hash algorithm as the old one, which is given by the digestAlgorithm field of the Archive Timestamp or, if that optional field is not set, by the timestamp itself.

In a hash-tree renewal, the Archive Timestamp and the archived data objects it covers must be hashed and timestamped again. A new secure hash algorithm H is selected. The data objects referred to by the initial Archive Timestamp, those still present and not deleted, are hashed to give h(i). For each data object, the encoded Archive Timestamp Sequence, the concatenation of all previous Archive Timestamp Chains in chronological order related to that data object, is hashed to give ha(i). Each h(i) is concatenated with ha(i) and hashed again to give h(i)', and a new Archive Time Stamp is built for each of those values. A new chain holding the new Archive Timestamp is created and appended to the Archive Timestamp Sequence. Archive Timestamps that are not necessary for verification should not be added to a chain or a sequence.

Verification of the whole structure has three parts. The first Archive Timestamp of the first chain must contain the hash value of the data object. Each chain is then verified: the first hash value list of each Archive Timestamp must contain the hash value of the timestamp of the Archive Timestamp before it, each Archive Timestamp must be valid relative to the time of the following Archive Timestamp, and all the Archive Timestamps within a chain must use the same hash algorithm, which must be secure at the time of the first Archive Timestamp of the following chain. Finally, for all the other chains, the first hash value list of the first Archive Timestamp must contain a hash value of the concatenation of the data object hash and the hash value of all the older chains, and that Archive Timestamp must have been generated before the last Archive Timestamp of the previous chain became invalid. To complete the proof, the last Archive Timestamp has to be valid at the time the verification is performed.
sections.plainLanguage: A chain is a series of timestamps where each new one covers the previous one, so the proof survives the failure of the older timestamp. A sequence is a series of chains, where a new chain covers the data and all the older chains, so the proof survives the failure of the older hash algorithm. Checking the whole thing means recomputing the hashes at every level and confirming that each link was made while the previous one was still good.

sections.title: Encrypted Data and Re-Encryption
sections.content:
If a service provider archives data and generates the Archive Timestamps, clients may want to send only encrypted data. That means the evidence records refer to encrypted data objects. ERS directly protects the integrity of the bit stream, which freezes the bit structure at the time of archiving and precludes changing the encryption scheme during the archival period. If the scheme is no longer secure, a change is not possible without losing the integrity proof of the Evidence Record, and the services of a data transformation, and with it a possible re-encryption, done by a notary service might be a solution. Two precautions follow.

Evidence generated to prove the existence of encrypted data cannot always be relied on to prove the existence of unencrypted data, because it may be possible to choose an algorithm or a key for decryption that is not the algorithm or key used for encryption. Only encryption methods should therefore be used that make it possible to prove that archive-timestamped encrypted data objects unambiguously represent unencrypted data objects, and all the data necessary for that proof should be included in the archived data objects.

When a relying party uses an evidence record to prove the existence of encrypted data objects, it may be desirable for clients to store only the unencrypted data objects and delete the encrypted copy. In order to use the evidence record, it must then be possible to unambiguously re-encrypt the unencrypted data to get exactly the data that was originally archived, so additional data necessary for re-encryption should be inserted into the evidence record by the client, which means the archive service never sees those values.

The EncryptionInfo field holds the information necessary for the unambiguous re-encryption of unencrypted content so that it exactly matches the encrypted data objects protected by the Evidence Record. Its syntax is a sequence of an object identifier naming the encryption method and a value of any type defined by that identifier, with a different form for the 1988 and the 1997 ASN.1 syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Archived files may be encrypted, and the record then proves the existence of the encrypted bytes. If a client wants to keep only the readable copy, the record must carry what is needed to turn it back into exactly the bytes that were archived, and that material has to be added by the client, so the archive never sees it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section has four parts. The first is secure algorithms: the cryptographic algorithms and parameters used within Archive Timestamps must be secure at the time of generation, which concerns the hash algorithm used in the hash lists as well as the hash algorithms and public key algorithms of the timestamps, and publications about the security suitability of cryptographic algorithms have to be considered by the verifying components.

The second is redundancy. Retrospectively, certain parts of an Archive Timestamp may turn out to have lost their security suitability before this has been publicly known, for example because algorithms have lost their security suitability, or even because the timestamping authorities themselves are untrustworthy, and this can result in Archive Timestamps losing their probative force. Many authorities use the same signature algorithms, so the compromise of a private key will only affect the security of one specific authority, while the retrospective loss of security of a signature algorithm affects a potentially large number of authorities at once. To counter such risks it is recommended to generate and manage at least two redundant Evidence Records with Archive Timestamp Sequences using different hash algorithms and different authorities using different signature algorithms, and to manage the Archive Timestamps in a central long-term archive.

The third is secure timestamps. Archive timestamping depends on the security of normal timestamping, so the security requirements for timestamping authorities stated in security policies have to be met. Renewed Archive Timestamps should have the same or higher quality than the initial Archive Timestamp, and Archive Timestamps used for signature renewal of signed data should have the same or higher quality than the maximum quality of the signatures.

The fourth is secure encryption. For a non-repudiation proof it does not matter whether the encryption has been broken or not, but users should keep their private keys and the randoms used for encryption secret, disclosing them only if needed, for example to a judge or an expert in a lawsuit, and they should use encryption algorithms and parameters that are expected to be unbreakable as long as the confidentiality of the archived data matters.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things have to be watched: that the algorithms in use are still considered safe, that the record is not the only copy, and that the timestamping service itself is trustworthy. The RFC therefore recommends keeping two records built with different hash algorithms and different timestamping authorities.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF AN ARCHIVE TIMESTAMP

items.title: digestAlgorithm
items.text: The hash algorithm used in the reduced hash tree. If it is absent, the digest algorithm of the timestamp is used.

items.title: attributes
items.text: Information an archive may want to provide about individual renewal steps and applied policies.

items.title: reducedHashtree
items.text: The lists of hash values, grouped into partial hash trees, that are needed to verify a single data object.

items.title: timeStamp
items.text: The timestamp itself, for example as a TimeStampToken in the RFC 3161 format.
